To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

δ13Cbreathing of insectivorous bats is depleted in 13 C in comparison toδ 13C of the ingested insects, and that δ13Cbreaths of satiated bats levels off at –2‰ in relation to theδ 13C signature of the ingested food.

δ13Cbreaths of fasting and satiated birds and mammals are depleted by 3.2 and 0.5‰ in relation to δ13Cdiet, respectively, and that the residence time of exogenous substrates in the pool of endogenously combusted substrates is species- and substrate-dependent.

the carbon isotope ratio in exhaled breath (δ13C breath) is sensitive to the type of ingested food and that the isotopic signature in exhaled breath of satiated individuals can level off at values similar, but slightly enriched, to that of the dietary isotope composition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of δ13C breath as a tracer for the dietary analysis in small birds and mammals.
the residence time of 13C in metabolized substrates in bats and the effect of endogenous substrates on the carbon isotope ratio in exhaled CO2 of satiated individuals.
the correct interpretation of stable carbon isotope ratios in exhaled breath of free-ranging birds and mammals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

δ 13C of exhaled breath is a suitable tool for the non-invasively collection of dietary information of free-ranging mammals and birds, if (i) the isotopic signature and the composition of ingested food items is known, (ii) the residence time of exogenous carbon atoms in the metabolized pool is determined, (iii) the residence time in the metabolized substrate pool is known, (iv) the isotopic equilibrium between endogenous and exogenous substrates is known,
δ13Cbreaths of birds and mammals can be used as an indicator of dietary information, if endogenous substrates are in isotopic equilibrium or not used for combustion.

the difference betweenδ 13Cdiet and δ13Cbreth of satiated animals can be predicted by the rate of metabolism of the combusted macronutrients, but not the isotopic composition of the endogenous substrate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the difference betweenδ 13Cdiet and δ13Cbreaths of fasting animals is an indicator for the rate at which the pool of metabolizable substrates is refilled by the ingested food, and δ13C breath of satiated animals is an indicator of whether or not endogenous substrates are in isotopic equilibrium to exogenous substrates.

δ 13C of exhaled CO is a reliable tracer for dietary information, but the interpretation ofδ 13C in free-ranging animals is not trivial, especially if the isotopic signature in exhaled CO2 is not in equilibrium with the dietary isotope signal.
δ 13C in exhaled breath of satiated birds and small mammals levels off at values that are close to theδ 13C signature of their ingested food.
The main takeaway from our work is that
δ13Cbreathtakes longer than 24 h to reflectδ 13Cdientirely in free-ranging birds and mammals, which is a key finding for the interpretation ofδ 13C breath in free-ranging animals.

the isotopic signature (δ13C) of the exhaled CO2 of free-ranging animals is sensitive to changes of ingested food items, and to the mixed combustion of endogenous and exogenous substrates, and that the isotopic offset betweenδ 13C of exhaled CO 2 and the diet is dependent on the type of ingested food.

the isotope signature of the exhaled CO2 of free-ranging animals can be used as a non-invasive tracer of the dietary carbon isotope ratio, but the isotope signature in the exhaled CO 2 of recently fed animals is a composite signal of both exogenous and ingested substrates.
